issues.legal_issue: The provision governing common village property does not vest property in a village authority merely because villagers use it in common when the authority's ownership or administration of that property is not established.
material_facts: Villagers used the tank water for drinking and for their cattle, and had acquired a prescriptive right to that use.
The village authority did not claim, and the courts had not found, that it owned or administered the property or its income for the villagers’ common benefit.
issues.conclusion: The common-property provision was not attracted on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 64 of the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, applies to property or income that belongs to or has been administered for villagers in common. The Court held that communal use alone did not satisfy the relevant requirement in this case.

predicates.communal_use_of_property: Villagers used the property or its income for a shared community purpose.
predicates.authority_ownership_or_administration_es: The village authority owned the property or administered it for the community’s benefit.

issues.definition: When villagers use property in common but the village authority’s ownership or administration of it is not established, the common-property vesting provision does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory vesting of a public water source and its non-private appurtenant land in a village authority confers control and supervision, not absolute title, and remains subject to public prescriptive rights and government power to assume management.
material_facts: Villagers dug the tank and used its water for drinking and for their cattle over a long period, thereby acquiring a prescriptive right to use it.
The tank was a public tank, and the land appurtenant to it was not found to be private property.
The village authority took possession and exercised control and supervision over the tank and its land.
issues.conclusion: The tank and qualifying appurtenant land vested in the village authority for control and supervision, not with absolute title; government management remained possible subject to the villagers’ prescriptive rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 85(1) of the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, covers public waterworks, including those used by the public to an extent giving a prescriptive right, and non-private appurtenant land. Sections 85(2) and 85(3) address the authority’s use of the works and land and the government’s power to limit its control or assume administration. The Court approved Gram Panchayat, Mandapaka v. District Collector, Eluru, AIR 1982 AP 15, and overruled Anna Narasimha Rao v. Kurra Venkata Narasayya, [1981] AWR 325. In explaining the contextual meaning of vesting, it also referred to Fruit and Vegetable Merchants Union v. Delhi Improvement Trust, [1957] SCR 1, and Port of London Authority v. Canvey Island Commissioners, [1932] 1 Ch. 446.

predicates.statutory_vesting_interpretation_case: The case concerns the legal effect of statutory vesting of a public water source in a village authority.
predicates.public_water_source_used_to_prescriptive: The public used the water source to an extent that gave the public a prescriptive right to use it.
predicates.appurtenant_land_not_private: The land adjacent or appurtenant to the water source was not private property.

issues.definition: When a statutory vesting case concerns a publicly used water source and non-private appurtenant land, the village authority receives control and supervision rather than absolute title.

issues.legal_issue: A ryotwari patta granted in individuals’ names does not give them personal beneficial title when the underlying inam grant was for maintaining a public tank and the land was held for that institution.
material_facts: The inam register described the grant as being for preserving and repairing the tank, and survey records identified the tank as a village tank and the land as village poramboke.
The tank was dug by villagers and used by them as a public water source.
A ryotwari patta was granted to the grantee’s descendants in their individual names and became final after an appeal.
The descendants enjoyed income from the property but did not repair or maintain the tank.
issues.conclusion: The grant was for the tank institution, not for the descendants’ personal benefit; the individual pattas did not give them personal rights in the property, which vested in the village authority for control, management, and supervision.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 7 of the A.P. Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, the relevant inquiry includes whether inam land in an inam village is held by an institution; where it is held by an institution, the patta entitlement is for that institution. The Court relied on the evidentiary value of the Inam Fair Register and survey and settlement records, followed K.V. Krishna Rao v. Sub-Collector, Ongole, [1969] 1 SCR 624, and approved Nori Venkatarama Dikshitulu v. Ravi Venkatappayya, [1959] 2 A.W.R. 357, which held that trustees cannot derive personal advantage from trust property merely because a patta is in their names. The property’s vesting and the extent of the village authority’s rights were governed by section 85 of the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, 1964.

predicates.inam_grant_for_public_tank_maintenance: The land was granted to support the preservation or maintenance of a public tank.
predicates.ryotwari_pattta_in_individual_names: A landholding patta was issued in the names of individuals who held or claimed the land through the grant.
predicates.public_tank_institution: The tank was a public water source treated as the institution for whose benefit the land was held.

issues.definition: Where land granted to maintain a public tank is held for the tank institution, an individual patta does not give its named holders personal beneficial title.

issues.legal_issue: A public tank is not treated as a public trust requiring the removal of its alleged hereditary trustees under the religious endowments removal procedure merely because land was granted for its preservation and maintenance.
material_facts: The tank was found to be a public tank dug by villagers and used by them for water.
The land grant was for preserving and maintaining the tank.

The lower court had characterized the tank as a public trust and considered the descendants hereditary trustees, but the Supreme Court held that the tank remained a public tank rather than a public trust.
issues.conclusion: The religious endowments legislation did not apply, and no proceeding to remove the descendants as trustees was required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 77 of the A.P. Hindu Charitable and Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, provides a procedure for removal of trustees where applicable. The Court held that the provision was inapplicable because the tank was a public tank, not a public trust. It relied on the finding about the tank’s public character and the grant’s purpose.

predicates.trustee_removal_dispute: A party claims that a person managing property must first be removed as a trustee before possession or control can be taken.
predicates.public_water_source_not_public_trust: The property is a public water source, and the court finds that it is not a public trust.

issues.definition: When a dispute seeks removal of alleged trustees but the water source is found not to be a public trust, the trustee-removal procedure is not required.

issues.legal_issue: Civil courts cannot retry or grant relief that sets aside or modifies a final decision on ryotwari patta under the inam legislation, except where the decision was obtained by fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion.
material_facts: The revenue authority granted ryotwari patta to the descendants, and the decision was confirmed on appeal and was not further challenged.

The inam legislation provided for determination of patta entitlement, appeals and revision, and finality of decisions, while expressly preserving an exception for decisions obtained by fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion.
The dispute included civil suits asserting rights to possession based on the property and the patta.
issues.conclusion: The inam legislation is a self-contained code that excludes civil jurisdiction over suits which would directly nullify a patta decision, except on the stated grounds of fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is subject to express or implied statutory exclusion. Sections 3, 7, 13, 14, 14-A, and 15 of the A.P. Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, establish the patta determination and review scheme, bar civil suits to set aside or modify covered decisions except for fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion, and give the Act overriding effect. The Court applied the principles in Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1968] 3 SCR 662, and Desika Charyulu v. State of A.P., AIR 1964 SC 807, and approved D.V. Raju v. B.G. Rao, [1961] 2 A.W.R. 368. It held P. Pedagovindayy v. Subba Rao, [1969] 2 A.L.T. 336, not to be good law.

rule.if: civil_suit_under_special_patta_regime and tribunal_finally_decided_patta_entitlement and civil_relief_would_set_aside_or_modify_decision and not fraud_misrepresentation_or_collusion

predicates.civil_suit_under_special_patta_regime: A civil suit concerns rights determined under a special statutory regime for granting landholding pattas.
predicates.tribunal_finally_decided_patta_entitleme: The competent statutory tribunal finally decided who was entitled to the patta, subject to the statutory review process.
predicates.civil_relief_would_set_aside_or_modify_d: The relief sought in the civil suit would directly set aside or modify the tribunal’s decision.
predicates.fraud_misrepresentation_or_collusion: The tribunal’s decision was obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion.

issues.definition: A civil court cannot grant relief that would undo a final patta decision under a special statutory regime unless the decision was obtained by fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion.

issues.legal_issue: Where land was granted to maintain a public tank, a final patta in individuals’ names did not entitle them to recover possession of property vested in the village authority, while the authority’s separate suit to obtain possession was unnecessary because it already had statutory control and possession rights.
material_facts: The village authority and the descendants each filed a suit for possession concerning the tank and its appurtenant land.
The descendants’ patta was granted in their individual names, but the grant was for maintaining the public tank.
The tank and its qualifying appurtenant land vested in the village authority for control, management, and supervision.
The village authority had taken possession and exercised control over the property, though it had done so without due process.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal of both possession suits was upheld: the village authority did not need a further decree for possession, and the descendants were not entitled to recover possession on the basis of their individual pattas.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 85 of the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, under which qualifying public waterworks and appurtenant land vest in the village authority for control and supervision, and sections 3 and 7 of the A.P. Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, in holding that the patta was for the tank institution rather than the named individuals personally. It also held that the statutory vesting left no need for a possession decree in favour of the village authority, although its taking of possession without due process was improper.

predicates.cross_suits_for_possession: The village authority and the persons claiming through the original grant each brought a suit seeking possession of the same property.
predicates.public_tank_land_vested_for_authority_co: The property is a public tank and qualifying appurtenant land vested in the village authority for control, management, or supervision.
predicates.patta_held_for_tank_institution: A patta issued to individuals concerns land held for the benefit of the tank institution rather than for their personal benefit.

issues.definition: When opposing possession suits concern land held for a public tank and vested in the village authority for control, a patta for the tank institution does not support recovery by the named individuals, and neither possession suit succeeds.
